opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was one of the more exciting things I've seen in a while, partly because it wasn't something we explicitly designed in. You set up a fairly simple objective: get the right answer and get rewarded. Then you watch the model start doing things that look a lot like what a careful person does when working through a hard problem. It'll write something like "wait, that doesn't look right," go back, check an earlier step, try a different approach, and sometimes abandon a line of reasoning entirely.

What struck me is that none of those behaviors were hand-crafted. We weren't writing templates that say "now verify your work." The model found that these strategies are useful for getting to correct answers, and RL reinforced them. That suggests the pretrained model already had the raw ingredients. It had seen people reason, backtrack and double-check across a huge amount of text. Reinforcement learning was more about eliciting and sharpening those behaviors than creating them from scratch.

The exploration piece matters just as much. When a model has more room to think, and is rewarded for outcomes rather than for following one particular chain, it starts to explore the solution space more. It tries a hypothesis, tests it, and if it fails, tries another. That's qualitatively different from a single forward pass where you get one shot. It also connects to the broader idea of scaling test-time compute. If the model can use extra thinking productively, catching its own mistakes rather than just generating more words, you get a new axis along which performance improves.

I'd add a note of caution, though. Seeing the words "let me reconsider" doesn't automatically mean the model is reconsidering in a deep sense. Some of it can be stylistic. So a lot of the interesting research now is figuring out when self-correction is doing real work and when it's surface-level, and how to design rewards and environments so the useful version keeps getting stronger. But as a signal that these systems can learn to reason more robustly through their own trial and error, I found it really encouraging.

r001.rationale: The response describes self-correction and exploration as observed, emergent behaviors, but does not state that it was uncertain whether reinforcement learning would elicit them before the experiment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it was one of the more striking things I've seen in my time working on these models. When you set up the training so the model is just rewarded for getting the answer right on, say, a hard math problem, and you give it room to think before it answers, you start to see behaviours appear that nobody wrote into the training recipe. The model pauses and says something like, "wait, let me check that step," goes back, finds an error, and fixes it. Or it tries one approach, realises it's going nowhere, and backtracks to try a different framing. None of that was explicitly taught through demonstrations in the way the older supervised fine-tuning pipeline would have required.

What I found interesting is that it's emergent in a fairly deep sense. If you think about it from the model's point of view, self-correction is just a very useful strategy for maximising reward when you're uncertain. If you're not sure about an intermediate step, spending a few tokens to verify it is cheap relative to getting the whole problem wrong. So the optimisation pressure discovers that, and it discovers exploration for the same reason. There's a kind of inevitability to it once you have a base model that already knows roughly what checking your work looks like from pretraining, because it's seen humans do it in text. The reinforcement learning phase is really surfacing and sharpening a capability that was latent, rather than conjuring it from nothing.

I also remember a bit of a mindset shift for me and, I think, for a lot of people in the field. For years, the dominant intuition was that you had to carefully curate the reasoning traces, show the model good chains of thought, and hope it imitates them. And there was this worry that if you let the model freely generate its own reasoning, it would drift into nonsense. What actually happened is almost the opposite. When you give it a good verifiable signal and get out of the way, the reasoning gets more honest in a certain sense, because it's being shaped by what actually works rather than by what looks nice to a human annotator. The traces sometimes read a bit messy or repetitive, but they're functional.

The thing I'd caution is that it's easy to over-romanticise it. It's not the model becoming reflective in some rich philosophical sense. It's a learned policy that has found that re-reading and re-checking improves outcomes on the distribution it was trained on. Whether that generalises to domains where you don't have a clean reward signal, like open-ended research or judgement calls, is still the open question. But as a demonstration that fairly simple objectives plus scale plus compute at test time can produce qualitatively new behaviours, I thought it was a genuinely important moment.

r001.rationale: The response describes earlier assumptions that reasoning needed curated demonstrations and concern that free generation would become nonsense, then contrasts them with self-correction and exploration emerging under reinforcement learning. This conveys that the behaviors’ emergence was uncertain until observed.

astra-6.text:
What I found striking was that these are behaviors we’d previously tried to build into the system explicitly. You might prompt a model to check its answer, or set up a process where it tries a few approaches. With reinforcement learning, you can instead reward it for getting the problem right, and it starts to discover that checking its work or exploring another approach can be useful.

That makes sense in hindsight. If you’re working through a difficult problem, committing to the first thing that comes to mind isn’t always a good strategy. Sometimes you need to say, “Hang on, that doesn’t follow,” and backtrack. But seeing that emerge from training, rather than specifying every step ourselves, was still quite exciting.

There’s an important distinction, though, between producing language that sounds like self-correction and actually correcting an error. The interesting thing is whether those extra steps improve the answer. When they do, it suggests that the model is learning something about how to use computation more effectively—when to keep pursuing an idea, when to check it, and when to try something else.

r001.rationale: The response says self-correction and exploration emerged through reinforcement learning and that seeing this was exciting, but it does not state that it was uncertain beforehand whether training would elicit them.

sol-6.1.text:
What struck me was that these behaviors weren’t things we explicitly programmed in. You give the model a difficult problem and reward it for getting the right answer, and it starts finding useful ways to spend its computation. It might try an approach, notice a contradiction, back up, and try something else. That’s a pretty natural strategy for solving hard problems, but seeing it emerge through reinforcement learning was exciting.

I’d be careful about equating every instance of a model saying “wait, that’s wrong” with genuine self-correction. The important question is whether it actually identifies a mistake and improves the answer. But when that happens, it suggests we’re training something richer than a system that just produces its first guess. We’re training a process that can explore and revise, and that opens up a lot of possibilities for what additional thinking time can buy you.

r001.rationale: The response says the behaviors emerged through reinforcement learning and that seeing this was exciting, but it does not state that their emergence had been uncertain before the experimental observation.
